Plotter Sketchpad v294 — FRONT PUDDLE OFF BY DEFAULT -- Street's Front puddle and Library's Front shine default to 0; turn the knob up for one big puddle (queue row 69)

Turn knobs. Reroll. When it looks like something, download the SVG.

Engine

Notes — what every control does

SVG out: stroke-width 0.3, black, no fills. The page is a RECTANGLE and has been since v186 — Page size is the SHORT axis, Page long the long one, and Page portrait stands the sheet up (all three in the Bed & fit fold). Both default to 200 mm, so an untouched page is square and behaves exactly as it always did. Every mm readout on this page is real millimetres on both axes: the page is scaled, never stretched, so a circle stays a circle at any aspect.
vpype --config funssor.toml read in.svg linemerge linesort gwrite -p funssor out.gcode

The 36 engines — which one to reach for

One engine draws at a time; Pin layer below is how you get two. Grouped as the tabs are. Everything here is what the engine draws and the one thing about it that surprises people; the knobs themselves are documented on their own rows behind i.
DISCS. Record: a vinyl disc — concentric grooves, an epicyclic wobble, and damage. The cut, the freed wedge, the fray, the sag, the drip and the inlaid word are all one engine, which is why it has more knobs than anything else here. Moiré: one continuous path swept along a 3D spine; the depth you read is interference between neighbouring passes, so it is the one engine linesimplify destroys. Geometric chuck: the rose-engine model, one unbroken path — a circle whose centre rides an epitrochoid while its radius is harmonically modulated. Phyllotaxis: golden-angle seed packing; Arms connects every n-th seed, so Fibonacci values give the arms a sunflower actually has. Log spiral: equiangular spiral, several arms. Growth per turn also decides whether a rotated copy nests or lands back on the original. Chladni disc: a round plate’s Bessel modes — not the square plate with its corners cut off, which is a different set of shapes entirely. Apollonian: Descartes circle packing, every gap filled by the circle tangent to its three neighbours. Every circle is its own closed path, so Min radius is the pen-lift budget.
RIDGES. Fingerprint: an orientation field with singularities — a core and a delta — combed into ridges. A print is a pattern of DIRECTIONS, not of lines, and the singular points are what make one look real.
FIELDS. Flow field: the Fidenza construction — trace curves through a grid of noise angles. Contours: marching squares over a noise field; a topographic map of a landscape that does not exist. Ridgeline: stacked noise profiles with hidden-line removal — the Joy Division sleeve. The occlusion is the whole effect. Interference: N point sources radiating sines, summed and then contoured. Unlike a moiré, which beats at a period fixed by construction, this one’s fringes vary across the page. Growth: differential growth — a closed loop whose nodes repel, attract along the loop and smooth, inserting new nodes until it runs out of room and buckles. Fully deterministic, so Reroll does nothing to it.
LATTICES. Truchet: quarter-arc tiles dropped in random orientation; the curves join across tile edges into long continuous runs. Maze: recursive division, drawn as walls. Hilbert: the space-filling curve, one continuous line. It is the one engine that does not gain cells on a wider page — the lattice is n×n with n a power of two, so it centres instead. Voronoi: half-plane clipping with Lloyd relaxation; relaxation is what turns scattered seeds into an even, organic-looking mosaic. Packing: circles grown from random seeds until they collide. Attempts scale with page area, so a bigger sheet gets more discs rather than the same ones larger.
CURVES. Harmonograph: two damped pendulums, one continuous line. Superformula: Gielis’ one equation, which degenerates to circles, squares, stars, flowers and a great many shapes with no name. L-system: a grammar rewritten n times and walked with a turtle — structure lives in the production rules, not in any coordinate. The first five grammars are one enormous unbroken stroke; the last two branch, so they fragment at every bracket. String art: chords from point i to i×mult; every line is straight and the curve is their envelope. Fan: one precessing ellipse carrying the Moiré camera. Chladni: the square plate’s nodal lines, contoured.
FROM PHOTO. These three need an image — open MASK & PINS and load one, or the page draws nothing and says so. Tone hatch: the polargraph portrait — rows of zigzag whose swing follows local darkness. One continuous stroke per row, no pen lifts, tone from line density. Tone spirals: dart-thrown circles sized by local lightness, each filled with an Archimedean spiral whose pitch follows the tone under it. Iso from photo: the picture becomes the solid — the image’s grey is read as height over an isometric grid, so you get a 3D form out of a photo without authoring any shapes.
3D. These nine share one camera (Yaw, Pitch and the rest) and one hidden-line pass, and the occlusion is usually the point rather than a finish. Iso city: an isometric city on a grid — the engine cousin of isocity.py. Plazas is the knob that makes a dense grid plottable: it is negative space and it cuts the path count at the same time. Hilbert 3D: Skilling’s curve in three dimensions, flattened by cutting rather than by tone. Harmonograph 3D: the third pendulum turns a flat lissajous into a knotted ribbon with unambiguous depth ordering. Attractor: Lorenz, Aizawa, Thomas and Halvorsen — four different systems with their own equations, not four presets, so a step size that suits one will blow another up. Ruled surface: the hyperboloid, built entirely from STRAIGHT segments, which is the ideal case for a pen. Torus knot: a (p,q) knot; the most legible object here, and the right thing to check the hidden-line pass against because you can see the over-under. Sphere pack: packed spheres drawn as latitude rings. Spheres are surfaces and the shared occluder only knows curves, so this engine hides its own far sides before the shared pass runs. Flow 3D: streamlines through the CURL of a noise potential. Divergence-free, which is why the lines do not all pile into the same sinks. Surface: parametric wireframes — torus, Klein bottle, trefoil tube, Möbius band, sphere. It opens on the trefoil because Torus knot next door is already a torus.

Plot-time estimate is pen-down only at 1000 mm/min — it ignores travel, so linesort matters. Single-path engines (Growth, Hilbert, Harmonograph, Moiré) have no travel at all — for those, linemerge linesort are no-ops and can be dropped.
Chladni / Chladni disc: contours are stitched into continuous polylines before export, so linesort alone handles the rest. Do not raise linemerge tolerance — separate nodal contours are meant to stay separate.
String art: chords from point i to point i × mult round a circle. Every stroke is straight; the curve is their envelope. Mult 2 is a cardioid, 3 a nephroid.
Phyllotaxis: golden-angle seed packing. Arms connects every nth seed into a path, so Fibonacci values give the arms a sunflower actually has.
Log spiral: rotating one about its pole is the same operation as scaling it, so a copy lands back on the original instead of beside it. Measured at a 1.33° step that only bites at high Growth — 0.44 mm apart at 400% per turn, against 1.19 mm at the default 60%. Under roughly one pen width the pens stack. Node on the pole and Growth up to nest; node off the pole to fan.
Reroll: only some engines consult the seed. Growth is fully deterministic; Hilbert only uses it when Warp is up; Fan only when End size is off 100 or Wobble is up. The button greys itself out when the current settings make it a no-op, instead of pretending.
Resets: the ↺ at the end of a row returns that one knob to its default — double-clicking the label does the same. It fades out when the knob is already there, so what is dimmed is what you have not touched. Reset all puts every engine, the Copies stage and the seed back to factory; it arms on the first click and fires on the second.
Scroll to nudge: point at any slider or number box and scroll — one wheel notch moves it one step, hold Shift for ten. The page does not scroll while you are over a control.
Tap i for what it does: every parameter that has a definition carries a small i at the end of its row — tap it and the note opens, tap again to close. It is a click toggle rather than a hover tooltip because hover does not exist on a phone, and this page is used on one. A row with no i has no note yet rather than a broken one.
Fan: one continuous precessing ellipse, built to be sparse enough that rotated copies stay legible. It carries the same camera as Moiré — Bend, Twist, Lift, Bulge, Winding drift, Yaw and Pitch all behave the way they do on that tab. All of them are zero at default, which is the flat disc. Projection is orthographic, so Lift and part of Bend are pure depth and do nothing at Yaw 0 / Pitch 0 — turn the camera before reaching for them. Moiré ships with Yaw already at 58 for the same reason.
Typed inputs: every slider has a number box beside it — type an exact value and press Enter or tab out. Values are clamped to the slider range and snapped to its step. Slider positions now persist when you switch engine tabs.
Presets: Save preset writes a .json holding the engine, the seed, and every slider on every engine. Load preset restores all of it, and named browser slots keep presets in this browser for quick recall. The slots vanish with site data and the file does not, so keep the .json beside the SVG it produced. If storage is unavailable the slot controls hide themselves and the file half keeps working.
Palette: the copies cycle through whichever pen set you pick — Spectrum is only the default. Mono gives you the fan geometry with no colour at all.
Mirror: reflects every second copy across a line through the node before rotating it, which is the mirror-moiré case: fringes concentrate along the axis and fan away from it. Watch the mirror gap readout: it is the average distance from the mirrored copy’s ink to ink already on the page. Under two pen widths, the second pass is filling, not interfering.
Copy scale — and why Step cannot skew a mirror: in 2D, Rot(t)·Ref(A) = Ref(A + t/2). A reflection composed with a rotation is still a reflection, about an axis swung by half the rotation — determinant stays −1 and the map stays an exact isometry at every value of Step. So with Mirror on, Step moves the hard axis and never produces a beat. The skew has to come from Copy scale: each copy is scaled by (1 + s)^k about the node, so Ref(A)×1.03 is a similarity with determinant −1 and magnitude ≠ 1. It keeps the mirror’s hard axis and fanning while adding a slowly-varying radial drift across the whole field. The stat line reports edge skew: how far the outermost copy has walked at the outer radius. Below one pen width the scale is doing nothing.
Hilbert 3D: the space-filling curve in three dimensions (Skilling’s algorithm), projected to the page. Flattening it is the whole problem — a screen fakes depth with tone, a pen has one weight per pass — so the depth is recovered by cutting: segments are processed near to far against a growing set of nearer ones, and wherever a strand passes within Occlusion gap of something in front of it, that stretch is dropped. The breaks in the far strands are the cue. Set the gap to 0 for the honest unbroken tangle, which is one continuous path. Note the default view is 30/25, not isometric: true isometric is the worst angle here, because the lattice axes align and the occluder correctly deletes all but the frontmost of every stacked edge — 54% of the curve survives there against 86% nearly face-on.
Mask from pins — a pen that will not draw on wet ink: the mask does not have to come from a file. Mask from pins rasterises the pinned layers and makes the drawing you already have into the keepout for the next one. With Pin mask width wide that is a silhouette. Near your actual pen width it is something more physical: pin pen 1, mask from pins, Mask 1, Halo one pen width, and pen 2 cannot land on pen 1 — not by care, by geometry. Two wet pens on one sheet is a real problem and nothing else in this toolchain solves it. Registration is exact rather than lucky: the unit square is rasterised into a square canvas, and the mask fit over a square reduces to the identity.
Pin layer: one engine at a time is baked into this app — mode picks a single builder. Pin layer freezes what is on screen as an underlay that survives a change of engine, so Hilbert over a mirrored Moiré is: build the moiré with Copies 2 and Mirror on, press Pin, switch to Hilbert, tune it against the moiré showing through at 55% underneath, then export. Pins write first, one <g> per pen, and they force the multi-pen export path even at Copies 1. A pin is frozen deliberately: Reroll, the palette and the global knobs no longer touch it. Each engine is fitted to its own bounding box, so layers both fill the page rather than sharing a coordinate system — right for a background/foreground pair, wrong if the two layers are meant to be the same object twice.
Engine layers — the engine gets a say in which pen draws what: every other way of getting more than one pen out of this page is something done to a finished drawing — Pens copies it, Pen map cuts it into bands, a pin freezes it. All three treat the engine's output as one undifferentiated pile of lines, which it usually is. Iso is the exception: it knows, at the moment it makes each solid, that the street grid is ground, that a roof mast or a silo cap or a rooftop plant room is accent, and that everything else is structure — the same three names isocity.py writes and plot -M reads. It used to throw that away. Engine layers keeps it: three <g> elements, pen01-ground / pen02-structure / pen03-accent, three passes on the plotter, and the swatch row becomes three pens whose colours are the ones the file carries. That accent register is where the reference photographs get their apparent density — every mast and dish and sign reads as a separate object because it is a separate colour, and the same geometry on one pen reads as texture. It replaces Pens and Pen map rather than composing with them, because pen 4 of a four-copy fan of three layers is “copy 2's accent”, which no pen setup can express. It changes nothing about what is accent — the engine's own Accent knob still decides that — only whether the split reaches the paper. Off on every other engine, and off by default, where the export is byte-for-byte what it always was. Turn Detail up to 3, or the accent pen has nothing to draw: all three accent draws sit behind detail ≥ 3 and Detail defaults to 1, so the layer is built and correctly empty. That gate is the engine’s and predates all of this. At Detail 3, seed 41, grid 8 the split is ground 9 / structure 3166 / accent 190 — 51 accent solids on their own pen.
Mask — and why Warp comes first: load any image and the darker side becomes the subject. It is thresholded (Otsu picks the starting value), then an exact euclidean distance transform is run over the result, so Halo is a comparison against a field that already exists rather than a re-cut — which is why it drags live. Mask 1 keeps what is outside the subject, 2 keeps what is inside. The stage order is engine → copies → warp → mask and that is not optional: Warp moves every point, so running it after the cut pushes lines back across the keepout by up to the full amplitude — at 12 mm that is three times a 4 mm halo. Same rule as the CLI chain in homelab/plotters/mask-composite-workflow_v1.md, and this is the browser half of maskplot.py.
Geometric chuck: the rose-engine model, one unbroken path. Each loop is a circle whose centre rides an epitrochoid and whose radius is harmonically modulated; |p − q| sets the lobe count. The loop is an ellipse rotated by Precession each turn — the eccentric chuck — and that rotation is what makes the figure chiral. Leave Loop ecc at 100 and you get the symmetry trap for free: a circle’s ink is invariant under its own start angle, so Precession turns nothing visible and the figure comes out exactly mirror-symmetric. Same orbit model as homelab/plotters/knotgen.py.
Copies: rotates the whole drawing about the node point, one pen per copy. The drawing itself never moves when you drag the node — only the sheet the copies need grows, so the view is held still for the duration of a drag and refits once you let go. At Pens 1 it is a pass-through and the SVG is byte-identical to v5. Above 1, the sheet grows to the union bounding box and each pen becomes its own top-level group — split with plot … -M. Drag on the canvas to move the node.
Moiré: the 3D read is interference between adjacent passes and nothing else. Do not run linesimplify on it — shifting points kills the effect. Watch the pen-down estimate; this engine reaches hundreds of metres easily.
